Uganda. A landlocked country in East Africa, bordered by Kenya, Tanzania, Rwanda, the Democratic Republic of the Congo, and South Sudan. Straddling the equator and rich with volcanic soils and freshwater lakes, most notably Lake Victoria, Uganda has long been a crossroads of African trade, culture, and power. Its modern history is marked by colonialism, independence, political upheaval, and complex post-conflict recovery shaped by figures like Idi Amin.

Uganda is a landlocked nation entirely within the watershed of the Nile River, which originates at Lake Victoria on its southern border. It shares the vast Lake Victoria with Tanzania and Kenya. This lake is the world's second-largest freshwater lake and supports millions of people. Uganda is home to the East African Rift Valley, characterized by dramatic escarpments, volcanic peaks, and rift lakes. It was a British colonial possession until independence in nineteen sixty-two, shaped by protectorate rule and administrative divisions that prioritized resource extraction.

From nineteen seventy-one to nineteen seventy-nine, Uganda was ruled by the brutal dictator Idi Amin, whose regime killed an estimated one hundred thousand to five hundred thousand people and destabilized the entire region. Uganda is known for diverse wildlife including mountain gorillas in the southwestern forests and savanna ecosystems that rival neighboring national parks. The Rwenzori Mountains—the Mountains of the Moon—in the southwest contain Uganda's highest peak, Mount Stanley, which sits on the border with the Democratic Republic of the Congo. Kampala is the capital and largest city, built on rolling hills overlooking Lake Victoria and serving as a regional hub for East African commerce and culture.

Post-conflict recovery has made Uganda one of East Africa's more stable and economically dynamic nations, with growing agriculture, coffee exports, and tourism. Uganda is culturally diverse with over fifty ethnic groups. The Baganda people and their kingdom represent the largest and historically most influential group, with their own traditional governance structures that persist alongside the modern state.
